questions.stem: Using the values shown (tidal volume 500 ml, anatomic dead space 150 ml, frequency 15/min), what is the alveolar ventilation?

explanation.summary: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate = (500 - 150) x 15 = 5,250 ml/min. Total (minute) ventilation of 7,500 ml/min overstates gas exchange because ~150 ml per breath fills conducting airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate = (500 - 150) x 15 = 5,250 ml/min. Total (minute) ventilation of 7,500 ml/min overstates gas exchange because ~150 ml per breath fills conducting airways.

questions.stem: This figure plots the partial pressure of oxygen falling stepwise from atmospheric air (159) through alveolar gas and arterial blood down to mitochondria (5 mmHg). What concept does it illustrate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The oxygen cascade from ambient air to the mitochondria

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Bohr shift with rising CO2

choices.label: E
choices.text: The alveolar-arterial gradient reversal during exercise

explanation.summary: The stepwise decline in PO2 from inspired air through humidification, alveolar dilution, diffusion, venous admixture, and tissue diffusion down to mitochondria is the oxygen cascade—the sequential pressure drops driving O2 from atmosphere to cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stepwise decline in PO2 from inspired air through humidification, alveolar dilution, diffusion, venous admixture, and tissue diffusion down to mitochondria is the oxygen cascade—the sequential pressure drops driving O2 from atmosphere to cells.

questions.stem: This equation computes alveolar oxygen tension from inspired oxygen, barometric and water vapor pressures, and PaCO2 divided by the respiratory quotient. It is most directly used clinically to calculate which value?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oxygen content of arterial blood (CaO2)

explanation.summary: This is the alveolar gas equation. Solving for alveolar PO2 (PAO2) and subtracting measured arterial PO2 (PaO2) yields the A-a gradient, which helps distinguish causes of hypoxemia (e.g., shunt/V-Q mismatch versus hypoventilation).
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the alveolar gas equation. Solving for alveolar PO2 (PAO2) and subtracting measured arterial PO2 (PaO2) yields the A-a gradient, which helps distinguish causes of hypoxemia (e.g., shunt/V-Q mismatch versus hypoventilation).
